title: Hidden Interfaces: From Tribology to Triboelectricity
content: The hidden interface problem has been notoriously difficult to handle in tribology. In contrast to indentation which is relatively simple as it only requires one degree of motion, sliding as in tribological problems involves shear with at least two axes of force and often relative motion in three dimensions. The fundamental question is what takes place at the buried interface (where all the action is)? Is there glide of dislocations at the interfaces; to what extent is their fracture versus plastic or elastic deformation; is wear a simple atom-by-atom process or does it involve collective motion? While in-situ experiments date back to the seminal work of Gane and Bowden in 1968 [1], it was not until the advent of scanning probes that Kizuka et al in 1997 demonstrated the possibility to image sliding at the atomic scale [2]. Here a scanning probe tip (either STM or AFM) mimics the role of asperities at contacting surfaces. However, it was still some time before Arno Merkle (assisted by his father and encouraged by this author) was able to demonstrate more general tribological results, beyond the simple gold samples first studied [3, 4].
